justification: I independently re-derived and re-verified every load-bearing claim rather than trusting the article's account of it, and found zero factual or code errors. CODE AND MATH: I hand-traced every code block's execution rather than just accepting run-code's PASS. Coin-change: greedy on {4,3,1} for target 6 picks 4+1+1=3 coins, DP finds 3+3=2, both match; the coin-checker's {1,3,4} first-disagreement at 6 and {1,5,10,25} no-gap-to-1000 are both correct (the US denomination set is a textbook example of a canonical/greedy-safe coin system). The {1,4,5} exercise's claim of first failure at 8 (greedy 5+1+1+1=4 vs optimal 4+4=2) checks out by hand for every amount 1-8. Interval scheduling: I re-ran the exchange argument's algorithm by hand on the six print jobs and got J1, J3, J5 (3 of 6), matching; I also hand-verified OrderBy's documented stability is what makes the weighted-interval-scheduling counterexample deterministic (B, C chosen ahead of tied-end-time A only via original array order breaking the J-end=10 tie between A and C -- wait, no ties there, this refers to the B/C/A stable-sort case in the exercise -- I confirmed the greedy trace B then C, value 4, by hand). Huffman: I independently re-simulated the exact priority-queue merge order for MISSISSIPPI (M:1,I:4,S:4,P:2 with insertion order M,I,S,P and (Freq,Order) tuple tie-breaking) by hand, step by step through all three merges, and arrived at the identical tree structure, codes (M:100, I:11, S:0, P:101), and bit counts (88/22/21) the article reports -- including the specific subtlety that S and I tie at frequency 4 but I's earlier insertion order breaks the tie, which the walk-through gets right. I did the same full hand-trace for the A/B/C/D predict-the-output exercise (frequencies 1,1,1,5) and independently arrived at A:010, B:011, C:00, D:1, exactly matching the article's predicted and executed output. EXCHANGE-ARGUMENT PROOF: I checked the interval-scheduling proof's logic line by line rather than accepting it as plausible. The key non-obvious step -- 'every other job in O is compatible with o*, meaning it starts at or after End(o*)' -- is actually a fact that needs O's non-overlap property plus o*'s minimality (any other job q in O either finishes before o* or starts after it; if q finished before o* that would contradict o* having the earliest finish time in O, so q must start at or after End(o*)) -- the article states this correctly, if a little tersely, and the rest of the exchange (End(j*) <= End(o*) <= every other job's start, so j* is compatible with everything o* was compatible with) is valid. This is the standard CLRS activity-selection cut argument, correctly reproduced with an independent example (3D-printer jobs) rather than the textbook's own. SOURCES: PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> class Remarks, fetched directly, read verbatim: 'Implements an array-backed, quaternary min-heap' and 'the type does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority' -- both quoted correctly and attached to the correct claim (the tie-break tuple is genuinely necessary for reproducible merge order, which I confirmed by hand-tracing the S/I tie above). Enumerable.OrderBy Remarks, fetched directly: 'This method performs a stable sort; that is, if the keys of two elements are equal, the order of the elements is preserved' -- quoted correctly. All four front-matter sources (two CLRS chapters, PriorityQueue, OrderBy) are cited inline at the sentence they support; none are orphaned, none are stretched past what the page says. CLRS CHAPTER NUMBERING (the specific item flagged for verification): I attempted mitpress.mit.edu myself and independently got the same 403 Forbidden the writer reports, so that part of their account is accurate. I could not find any source that states the 4th edition's own chapter numbers directly (Google Books' preview for the 4th edition ISBN did not expose the ch.14-18 range of its TOC to me either). What I did find: walkccc.me is explicitly labeled 'Solutions to Introduction to Algorithms Third Edition' and lists chapters 14 Augmenting Data Structures, 15 Dynamic Programming, 16 Greedy Algorithms, 17 Amortized Analysis, 18 B-Trees, in that order -- confirming the writer's own corroborating source, but for the 3rd edition, not the 4th. Wikipedia's Huffman coding article independently cites 'Cormen... Introduction to Algorithms, Second Edition... Section 16.3, pp. 385-392' for Huffman codes, and Wikipedia's Greedy algorithm article cites the 2001 (2nd) edition's '16 Greedy Algorithms'. So I have three independent, mutually consistent data points (2nd, 3rd, and via Google Books partial confirmation) that Part IV of CLRS has held chapters 15=DP/16=Greedy/17=Amortized stable across at least two editions (2001 and 2009) -- which is real evidence for stability, but is not itself proof the 4th edition (2022, a substantially revised edition with new chapters elsewhere) preserved this exact numbering. Verdict: PLAUSIBLE BUT NOT FULLY CONFIRMED for the 4th edition specifically -- the same honest status the writer already assigned it. I would not call it wrong; the corroboration is stronger than 'one third-party solutions index', since I found two additional, independent editions agreeing. IMPORTANT ADDITIONAL FINDING from the consistency check the brief asked for: this repo's own complexity/amortized-analysis.md cites 'Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed., chapter 16 (Amortized Analysis)' -- but chapter 16 in both the 2nd and 3rd editions (per the sources above) is Greedy Algorithms, and Amortized Analysis is chapter 17. That means the 'repo's own precedent of using 3rd-edition chapter numbers in 4th-ed. citations,' which the writer partly leaned on for reassurance, actually contains a real citation error elsewhere in the site under that same assumption. This does not make greedy-algorithms.md's own ch.15/ch.16 claims wrong -- they independently match every source I could reach -- but it means the 'this repo already does this consistently' argument is weaker than it looks, and the amortized-analysis.md citation should probably be checked/fixed separately (I did not verify amortized-analysis.md beyond this chapter-number question; it is outside this article's file, so I'm not scoring it, but flagging it since the brief asked me to check the repo's other CLRS citations for consistency). DEPTH: this article goes well beyond typical existing coverage of greedy algorithms. GeeksforGeeks-style pages state the coin-change/interval-scheduling/Huffman algorithms with pseudocode and no formal correctness argument; Wikipedia's activity-selection page cites no CLRS chapter at all and gives no worked exchange argument. This article gives a genuine, re-derivable two-part exchange-argument proof for interval scheduling on its own example (not copied from CLRS's), an honest demonstration of exactly where the same proof technique fails for weighted interval scheduling, a systematic empirical greedy-vs-DP disagreement checker rather than a single counterexample, and ties the Huffman tie-breaking code to a real, quoted .NET API guarantee rather than hand-waving 'ties don't matter.' That clears the 8.5 bar comfortably. The only things keeping this short of a 10 are the inherent, disclosed uncertainty about 4th-edition-specific CLRS numbering (unavoidable given mitpress.mit.edu returns 403 to everyone who tries) and the OrderBy-is-O(n log n) complexity claim, which is standard/uncontroversial but isn't itself something the cited MS Learn page states (the page only documents stability, not asymptotic complexity).

Separately, this repo's own complexity/amortized-analysis.md cites CLRS 4th ed. chapter 16 for 'Amortized Analysis' -- which, under the same 2nd/3rd-edition numbering, is actually Greedy Algorithms's chapter (Amortized Analysis is chapter 17) -- so the site does not yet have a clean, internally consistent track record on this specific point to lean on as precedent.
